title: multi-node degraded scaling and failsafe runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working draft runbook for handling multi-node degraded states that require a combination of GPU replacement, node cordon/drain, cluster recovery steps, and temporary capacity additions. It is intended for on-call SREs and on-call engineers supporting Redwood Dedicated and Private clusters.

Goals:
- Restore serving capacity with minimal customer impact (latency and error-rate SLOs).
- Make safe, reversible changes while preserving job state where possible.
- Document triage decisions for fast post-incident review.

Quick summary flow (one-line):
1) Triage alerts -> 2) Stabilize traffic (route/fallback) -> 3) Isolate problem nodes (cordon/drain) -> 4) Add short-term capacity if needed -> 5) Replace/repair hardware or restart corrupt services -> 6) Verify and uncordon -> 7) Post-incident actions.

Key contacts and channels:
- Primary on-call SRE: #sre-oncall (Slack)
- Compute ops pager: pagerduty (SRE escalation)
- Hardware ops: @data-center-team
- Incident lead template: assign to SRE on-call, second to infra-release-engineering

Initial triage (first 10 minutes):
- Identify the alert fingerprint: metric (gpu_util, pod_eviction_rate, pod_restart_count, node_unavailable), timestamp, and affected AZ/zone.
- Check Redwood Console Routes: which model routes are impacted? Prioritize production routes with SLA.
- Look for correlated alerts: storage latency, network partition, kube-scheduler errors.
- If > 10% serving capacity lost or tail latency > 2x SLO, immediately enable fallback routes to cheaper model variants and reduce batching sizes (low-risk knob).

Stabilization actions (if immediate customer impact):
- Apply rate-limits and circuit breaker rules in the routing layer for affected API keys.
- Switch heavy routes to warm standby nodes or alternate regions (smart routing).
- If using Dedicated pools, trigger autoscale-burst (if configured) or open a capacity-add request.

Node isolation checklist (safe isolation pattern):
- Command: kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=accelerator in affected AZ to list candidates.
- Pick one node at a time unless complete zone failure.
- Cordon the node: kubectl cordon <node>  # prevents new pods
- Drain politely: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
  - If drain hangs on evictions, identify stuck pods: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> and check events for PDB blocking or stuck Terminating.
  - For PDB-blocked critical pods, consider manual eviction with --force only after explicit approval from incident lead.
- After drain, confirm no serving pods remain on the node (kubectl get pods -o wide -n inference-system --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>).

Hardware replacement (GPU cartridge or node-level):
- If hardware flagged as FAILED by telemetry (ECC errors, nvlink faults, or thermal trip), schedule physical replacement: open a hardware ops ticket and mark node as unschedulable.
- If on-prem: coordinate with data-center-team to do hot-swap following physical-swap checklist (ESD safe, powered maintenance mode, re-seat GPU, verify PCIe link).
- If cloud provider: follow provider-specific guidance (e.g., detach GPU, replace instance type, perform instance replacement).
- After physical replacement, verify kernel dmesg, nvidia-smi and run short synthetic inference workload (smoke test) to validate model correctness and latency.

Cluster recovery and safe re-introduction:
- Run node health checks: kubelet status, kube-proxy, nvidia-driver, container-runtime (docker/containerd), disk health.
- Reboot only if consistent with hardware-advice. If reboot required, coordinate with scheduler to avoid flapping.
- Uncordon when health checks pass: kubectl uncordon <node>.
- Monitor pod placement and warm cache behavior; allow KV cache to prime under reduced load.

Temporary capacity add (when demand exceeds available healthy capacity):
- Preferred: scale up a warm pool of compatible instance types (same or compatible GPU family) to receive traffic immediately.
- If warm pool unavailable, spin new nodes from pre-baked images with the inference runtime and model caches preloaded. Use the pre-warm script: /opt/inference/prewarm.sh --model-catalog <catalog-id> --version <v>.
- Avoid overprovisioning: coordinate with cost control if adding > 2x baseline capacity.
- Annotate the scale event in incident timeline with exact instance counts and expiry for auto-termination.

Degraded-I/O or network cases (special handling):
- If pods are failing due to NFS/remote storage latency, move ephemeral state to local disk where safe (short term only), or reschedule to nodes in a healthy zone.
- If NVMe saturation observed, stagger batch jobs and disable background maintenance tasks (index rebuilds, heavy logs) temporarily.

Safety guardrails and abort conditions:
- Do not forcibly delete pods belonging to a control-plane namespace without approval.
- Avoid --force evictions unless a node is confirmed unrecoverable and the cost of waiting exceeds SLO impact.
- If more than 25% of a zone's GPUs are failing simultaneously, escalate to on-call infra lead and consider cross-zone failover.

Key commands cheat sheet (for quick copy/paste):
- List nodes with GPUs: kubectl get nodes -l accelerator=gpu -o wide
- Cordon: kubectl cordon NODE_NAME
- Drain politely: kubectl drain NODE_NAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
- Force delete pod (last resort): kubectl delete pod POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE --grace-period=0 --force
- Check driver: nvidia-smi -q | head -n 40
- Check kernel errors: dmesg | egrep -i "nvrm|gpu|nvlink|pci" | tail -n 200

Post-incident checklist (first 24 hours):
- Record timeline with decisions and who approved evictions/replacements.
- Create a postmortem draft in Confluence with impact metrics (requests, error rates, p95/p99 latency) and attach logs.
- Mark any long-running mitigations (e.g., capacity reservations) and create follow-up tickets to unwind them.
- Run a regression test on a representative prompt set to ensure model output quality did not regress after cache warm-up or model fallback.

Retrospective primers (what to capture):
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence chain.
- What worked: automation, fallback effectiveness, pre-warm scripts.
- What didn’t: blockers during drain, permissions, missing hardware spares, runbook gaps.
- Action items: e.g., maintain 2 spare GPU cartridges per region, expand warm-pool to 10% baseline, add pre-approval for forced-eviction in emergency playbook.

Incident notes template (paste into timeline):
- 00:00 Alert: metric and threshold
- 00:02 Triage: initial owner and first actions (fallback enabled?)
- 00:15 Node isolation: node IDs cordoned and drained
- 00:40 Hardware ops engaged: ticket # and ETA
- 01:25 Capacity-add: instances added (type and count)
- 02:10 Recovery verification: smoke test results and uncordon times
- 03:00 Customer impact summary: percent requests failed and p99 delta

Open questions and TODOs (draft):
- Add automatic PDB-aware graceful eviction helper to reduce manual approvals.
- Add a safe unblocking path for long Terminating pods tied to CSI drivers.
- Define explicit cost threshold for triggering autoscale-burst vs. manual capacity add.

Appendix: short checklist for physical GPU swap (on-prem)
- Confirm node power state and perform ESD precautions.
- Evacuate workloads (cordon+drain).
- Power down PCIe riser if required.
- Replace GPU cartridge, re-seat connectors, check retention clip.
- Power up and watch dmesg for PCIe enumeration.
- Validate driver sees GPU (nvidia-smi) and run 2x synthetic model inferences at 1x and 4x batch.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep this doc short; split long procedural scripts into separate playbooks that can be executed.
- Coordinate with product-hosted-api before rolling fallbacks for certain high-sensitivity customers.

End of draft.
